newsitem.title: USA: Hurricane Danny nears second Gulf Coast landfall.
newsitem.headline: Hurricane Danny nears second Gulf Coast landfall.

text.p: Hurricane Danny lashed the U.S. coastline from Mississippi to the Florida Panhandle with high winds and torrential rains on Saturday as it crept toward a second landfall near Mobile.
At 5 a.m. EDT (0900 GMT), the National Weather Service said the eye of the storm was nearly stationary about 25 miles (40 km) off the Alabama coast, south-southeast of the city.

A minimal hurricane, Danny had maximum sustained winds of 75 mph (121 kph). But forecasters expected the system to be downgraded quickly to a tropical storm as it came ashore and its wind strength waned.
Hurricane warnings remained in effect from Gulfport, Mississippi, to Apalachicola, Florida.

Eyewitnesses in the beachfront community of Gulf Shores, Alabama, reported power and phone outages as daylight approached, with waves breaking over a seawall and winds sweeping debris into the streets.
Danny came ashore for the first time early on Friday in Louisiana, between Grand Isle and the mouth of the Mississippi River, before moving back into the Gulf on a lumbering northeasterly track.

The hurricane killed at least two people on Friday as it veered toward a second landfall. An elderly man had a fatal heart attack while securing his boat against rising waters in Pirate's Cove, Alabama. Another man was found dead in a swamped sailboat near Fort Morgan, Alabama.

Late on Friday high winds caused sporadic power outages and threatened to spawn tornadoes throughout the region. A seagoing tornado, known as a water spout, damaged boats and tore roofs off buildings in a marina near Orange Beach, Alabama. No injuries were reported.

But officials said the biggest worry was flash flooding near rivers, streams and saturated lowlands. Weather forecasts called for up to 20 inches (51 cm) of rain along the storm's track over the course of the weekend.
"There's going to be a lot of wind. But our primary concern is rainfall due to its slow movement," said David Eversole, who heads the National Weather Service office in Mobile.

Many coastal residents, long accustomed to more powerful storms, chose to ride out the hurricane and spent all day on Friday loading up on batteries and other household goods or nailing sheets of plywood over their windows.
One Alabama resident spray-painted his boarded-up home with the defiant message "Danny is a Wanna-be."

But others, including thousands of vacationers from the area's surrounding resorts, joined long lines at gas stations before venturing into a steady stream of traffic headed for inland hotels and Red Cross shelters.
"We're staying," said Vicki Bruce, a tourist from Lexington, Kentucky. "There's more danger getting hurt in a traffic jam than there is from this storm."
The governors of Mississippi and Alabama declared states of emergency on Friday, while authorities in southern Alabama issued a voluntary evacuation order for low-lying coastal areas.
All but one of the 11 floating casinos moored along the Mississippi coastline kept their doors open to a trickle of diehard gamblers and tourists.
"It's a little slower than normal, but it's been consistent all day," said Lori Hutzler, spokeswoman for the Isle Capri Casino in Biloxi, which is open 24 hours a day.
"Patrons went out to get their supplies and then came back to gamble," she said.
